Apple's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (year ended September 27, 2025; signed October 31, 2025) dates the following legal/regulatory developments to specific days or months in calendar year 2025. They appear in Item 3 (Legal Proceedings, p. 21) and in the regulatory-scrutiny risk factor (p. 17).

**April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act (two actions, same day)**
- The European Commission fined Apple €500 million in the Article 5(4) Investigation (how developers may communicate and promote offers to end users and conclude contracts with them for apps distributed through the App Store) and issued a cease-and-desist order requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed that decision.
- Also on April 23, 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) Investigation (whether Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces may violate the DMA). A final violation determination could bring a cease-and-desist order and fines up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales, plus additional fines for violating a cease-and-desist order.

**April 30, 2025 — Epic Games (U.S. District Court, Northern District of California)**
- The court found Apple in violation of the 2021 Injunction and enjoined it from imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app; from restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to outside purchases; or otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app.
- The court also denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. Apple appealed to the Ninth Circuit; its stay request was denied, but the Ninth Circuit agreed to expedited review.

**September 2, 2025 — Google search antitrust remedies (commercial-relationship matter)**
- The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, following its August 5, 2024 finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws, ordered certain remedies. The order remains subject to further proceedings before that court (which may change how the remedies are interpreted or applied, or add new ones) and to appeal by both the DOJ and Google. Apple notes that a reversal on appeal could lead to imposition of remedies the DOJ initially proposed — such as barring Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution — which could materially hurt Apple's licensing revenue.

**October 2025** (month only, no day stated) — Epic Games appeal
- The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments in Apple's expedited appeal of the April 30, 2025 decision.

Related dates outside calendar 2025 (for contrast, since they frame the above): the DMA investigations were opened March 25, 2024 and June 24, 2024; the DOJ/states antitrust suit was filed March 21, 2024; Apple's compliance filing under the 2021 Injunction was January 16, 2024, with its motion to narrow or vacate filed September 30, 2024; and Google's liability finding was August 5, 2024. The filing also states that Apple settled certain matters in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025 without material impact, and that other ordinary-course matters remain unresolved.

Fiscal 2024 figures from NVIDIA's Form 10-K (year ended January 28, 2024):

**Component detail (Note 10 – Balance Sheet Components, pp. 68–70)**
- Inventory provision recorded in cost of revenue: **$774 million** in fiscal 2024 — the write-down of inventory (raw materials, work-in-process, finished goods) to its net realizable value for excess or obsolescence.
- Expense recorded in cost of revenue for inventory purchase obligations in excess of current demand projections, supplier charges, and penalties for cancellations and underutilization: **approximately $1.4 billion** in fiscal 2024. This relates to noncancelable or capacity commitments for inventory, and to cancellation/underutilization penalties.

Relationship: the $774 million inventory provision plus the ~$1.4 billion purchase-obligation expense make up the $2.2 billion total, against which the $540 million release was recorded.

**Source:** NVDA_2023_10K.pdf (fiscal year ended January 29, 2023) — principally Item 1A "Risks Related to Regulatory, Legal, Our Stock and Other Matters" (pp. 28–29), Item 1 "Government Regulations" (p. 11), and Item 7 MD&A "Global Trade" and "Russia" (p. 37).

## Effects described as having occurred

1. **Sanctions and export controls blocked shipments into Russia, Belarus, and parts of Ukraine.** The filing states that "in response to the war in Ukraine, the United States and other jurisdictions imposed economic sanctions and export control measures which blocked the passage of our products, services and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine" (p. 28).

2. **NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia.** "In fiscal year 2023, we stopped direct sales to Russia" (p. 28; repeated in MD&A at p. 37).

3. **NVIDIA closed its Russian business operations.** "…and closed business operations in Russia," which occurred "later in the year" within fiscal 2023 (pp. 28, 37).

4. **End-customer sales in EMEA were hurt.** "Concurrently, the war in Ukraine has impacted end customer sales in EMEA and may continue to do so in the future" (p. 28). The past-tense "has impacted" is an effect already realized; the filing does not quantify it.

5. **New U.S. government license requirements covering Russia made operations and forecasting harder.** The Q3 fiscal 2023 rules "impact exports to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and Russia" of A100/H100 chips, DGX or other systems/boards incorporating them, and A100X. NVIDIA states that "the impact of the new license requirements is difficult to quantify, and it may be challenging for us to manage our operations and forecast our operating results due to these requirements" (p. 11; see also pp. 29, 37).

## Described as possibly having occurred

6. **Indirect sales through partners into Russia may have been lost.** "Direct sales to Russia in fiscal year 2022 were immaterial. Our revenue to partners that sell into Russia may have been negatively impacted due to the war in Ukraine" (p. 37). This is the one item framed as an unconfirmed past/possible past effect rather than a known one.

## Matters the filing frames only as future risk (excluded per your instruction)

- That the EMEA impact "may continue" and that further restrictions, broader AI-related export controls, deemed-export limits on R&D, foreign-government retaliation (including by China), license delays/denials, excess inventory, and competitive disadvantage "may"/"could" occur (pp. 28–29, 37).
- The requirement to transition certain operations out of China and Hong Kong, and resulting transitional costs (pp. 29, 37) — attributed to the China-focused restrictions rather than to the Ukraine response.
- Elevated cyber-attack vulnerability "during times of war or other major conflicts" (p. 23) and generic "acts of war or other military actions" disruption risk (pp. 22, 24) — stated as prospective exposure, not as an experienced Ukraine-related effect.

Within the body of Boeing’s 2024 Form 10-K—excluding the exhibits—the dividend-related dollar amounts are:

- **$58 million** — Mandatory convertible preferred stock dividends **accumulated during 2024**. This amount is deducted from net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders in the EPS calculation. Because the preferred stock was issued on October 31, 2024, this reflects only the portion of the year after issuance.
- **$72 million** — Cash dividends **declared in December 2024** on the mandatory convertible preferred stock, payable to holders of record on January 1, 2025 and paid in cash on January 15, 2025. This equals **$12.50 per preferred share**.
- **$345 million per year** — The amount of cash Boeing says it **expects to require, up to that level, each year** to pay dividends on the outstanding mandatory convertible preferred stock through its October 15, 2027 mandatory conversion date.

The **$58 million** and **$72 million** are therefore different measures: the first is the 2024 accumulated preferred dividend deduction for EPS, while the second is the dividend declared at year-end 2024 and paid in January 2025.

I found the TDR adoption disclosures in JPMorgan Chase's 2023 Form 10-K (Note 1, "Accounting standards adopted January 1, 2023," and Note 13, "Allowance for credit losses").

## Firm-wide amounts (the two headline figures)

Adopted January 1, 2023 under the **modified retrospective method**:

- **$587 million — net decrease to the allowance for credit losses.** This is the cumulative-effect adjustment (a pre-tax, balance-sheet adjustment) taken against the allowance at adoption. In the Note 13 rollforward it appears as the "Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle" line within the allowance for loan losses, so the same $587 million reduces the Firm's allowance for loan losses. It reflects eliminating the requirement to measure TDR allowances using a discounted cash flow (DCF) methodology and applying a non-DCF, portfolio-based approach to modified loans (except collateral-dependent and nonaccrual risk-rated loans, which continue under the asset-specific/DCF approach).

- **$446 million — increase to retained earnings, after-tax.** This is the retained-earnings benefit of the adoption, net of the related income-tax effect (the ~$141 million difference from the $587 million pre-tax allowance reduction). Note 1 and Note 13 both state the change was **"predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card."**

## Portfolio-segment breakdown of the $587 million

The Note 13 allowance table breaks the cumulative-effect adjustment (reduction to the allowance for loan losses) out by portfolio segment:

| Portfolio segment | Effect on allowance for loan losses (millions) |
|---|---|
| Consumer, excluding credit card | $(489) |
| Credit card | $(100) |
| Wholesale | $2 |
| **Total Firm** | **$(587)** |

So $589 million of the reduction came from the consumer portfolios (Consumer excluding credit card plus Credit card), partly offset by a $2 million increase in Wholesale.

## What each amount measures — summary

- The **$587 million** is the one-time, pre-tax cumulative-effect reduction to the allowance for credit losses / allowance for loan losses at January 1, 2023 (with its portfolio mix shown above), arising from moving modified troubled-borrower loans from an asset-specific DCF approach to a portfolio-based approach.
- The **$446 million** is the resulting after-tax increase to retained earnings from that same adoption (i.e., the $587 million allowance reduction net of tax), attributed predominantly to residential real estate and credit card.

The 10-K reports these effects at the Firm level and by **portfolio segment** (Consumer excluding credit card, Credit card, Wholesale); it does not provide a separate adoption effect by business segment (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM).

From Walmart's fiscal 2026 Form 10-K (year ended January 31, 2026), two amounts are given for the receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency swaps designated as cash flow hedges:

1. **$6,020 million — notional amount.** This is the aggregate notional (contract) amount of the swaps as of January 31, 2026, used to calculate the contractual cash flows exchanged under the contracts.

2. **$(920) million — fair value, in a liability position.** This is the aggregate fair value of the swaps at January 31, 2026, shown in the Note 7 derivatives table (primarily classified in "deferred income taxes and other" on the consolidated balance sheet). Item 7A restates this same figure as a liability position of **$0.9 billion**.
